subtitle: Explain what Minnesota law requires before guardianship, compare supported decision-making and other less restrictive alternatives, protect the rights a person keeps under guardianship, and support people's own decisions without giving legal advice.
audience: For DSD and DHS leaders, supervisors, policy and program staff, and lead workers whose work touches guardianship, decision-making support, service planning or materials for people with disabilities and their families.

lessons.title: What a court must find before guardianship
objectives: Explain the findings Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310 requires before a court appoints a guardian.
Distinguish a diagnosis, a family's concern or a professional's opinion from the legal finding of incapacity.
Explain why a guardianship order, not the fact of guardianship, defines who decides a particular matter.
Describe how DSD staff can counter guardianship as a default without giving legal advice.
lessons.teaching:
Guardianship moves some of a person's legal authority over their own life to someone else. Minnesota law treats that as a serious step and sets conditions before a court may take it. Under Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310, a court may appoint a guardian only if it finds by clear and convincing evidence that the respondent is an incapacitated person and that the person's identified needs cannot be met by less restrictive means, including appropriate technological assistance and supported decision making. The court must make specific findings, particular to the person, about why less restrictive alternatives would not meet those needs.

The definition carries much of the weight. Section 524.5-102 describes an incapacitated person as someone impaired to the extent of lacking sufficient understanding or capacity to make personal decisions, and unable to meet personal needs for medical care, nutrition, clothing, shelter or safety even with technological assistance and supported decision making. A diagnosis, a test score, a school's recommendation or a family's worry is not that finding. The petition itself must state, to the extent known, what less restrictive means have been attempted and considered, for how long, and why they are not sufficient (section 524.5-303). The Minnesota State Court Administrator's Office self-help sheet on alternatives puts the expectation plainly: before guardianship is sought, less restrictive alternatives should be seriously considered and meaningfully tried, as appropriate.

When a court does appoint a guardian, the order should be limited. Section 524.5-310 directs the court to grant only the powers needed to address the person's limitations and demonstrated needs, to favor orders that support maximum self-reliance and independence where feasible, and it provides that any power not specifically granted remains with the person. The same section lets the court treat a petition as one for a protective order, issue another appropriate order or dismiss the proceeding. So the statement that a person has a guardian never answers who decides a particular matter. The order does, and many orders leave important decisions with the person.

Practice often moves faster than the law. In its December 2025 final report to the Legislature on supported decision making, DHS reported that guardianship often operates as the default path, especially for young people with disabilities turning 18. Grantees found that many families and professionals understood the problems with guardianship but did not know other options existed, and one caller described being told by a teacher, a doctor, a social worker and a group home that guardianship was needed. DSD staff are part of that information environment. You are not assessing capacity and you are not giving legal advice. Legal, guardianship and eligibility decisions stay with the courts and the people or areas responsible, and a person or family with a legal question should be directed to their own attorney or to court self-help resources. What you can do is make sure people hear that alternatives exist, share neutral public information, and avoid wording in letters, forms and conversations that presents guardianship as the expected next step.
lessons.keyPoint: Minnesota law allows guardianship only on clear and convincing evidence of incapacity and specific findings that less restrictive means, including supported decision making, will not work. Powers the order does not grant stay with the person.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} is updating a DSD information sheet for families of young adults leaving school services. The current draft includes a checklist item that reads "Apply for guardianship before age 18." {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} asks {{SUPERVISOR}} whether to keep it, noting that several families have said the school told them it was required.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} advise?
choices: Replace it with neutral information that alternatives exist and must be considered first, with links to court self-help resources.
Keep the item, since families expect it and a checklist that leaves out guardianship might leave some young adults without needed protection.
Remove any mention of guardianship and alternatives, since the topic is legal and DSD staff should not discuss it with families at all.
feedback: This corrects a default the law does not support, keeps the sheet informational, and sends legal questions to resources built for them. It neither recommends nor rules out guardianship for any family.
The item presents guardianship as a routine step, which is the default the DHS report describes. Minnesota law requires that less restrictive means be considered and found insufficient first.

Avoiding legal advice is right, but silence leaves families with only the message they already heard. Sharing neutral public information about alternatives is not the same as advising someone what to file.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about how you first learned what guardianship is, or use the practice case. Was it described as a protection, a loss of rights, or a routine step, and how might that framing shape what you say to others?
lessons.action: Review one letter, form, web page or script your team uses with people or families. Mark any wording that presents guardianship as expected or required, and draft a neutral replacement that names alternatives and points to public court information. Bring it to the content owner.

check.question: Under Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310, what happens to a power the court does not specifically grant to a guardian?
check.correct: It remains with the person subject to guardianship.
wrong: It passes to the guardian once the order is signed.
It is held by the lead agency until the court rules again.
check.feedback: The statute provides that powers not specifically granted stay with the person. That is why staff need to know what an order actually says before they treat a guardian as the decision-maker on a given matter.

lessons.title: Alternatives and what each one actually authorizes
objectives: Describe supported decision making, health care directives, powers of attorney and representative payees as Minnesota and federal sources define them.
Explain the limits of each alternative, including which decisions it covers and when it takes effect.
Read the document or arrangement itself before treating someone as a decision-maker.
Recognize the system gaps that make alternatives harder to use for some people.
lessons.teaching:
Less restrictive alternatives are not one thing. Each covers different decisions, takes effect in different ways and carries different limits, and many people use more than one. Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-102 defines supported decision making as assistance from one or more people of the person's choosing in understanding the nature and consequences of personal and financial decisions, and, when consistent with the person's wishes, help communicating a decision once it is made. The State Court Administrator's Office describes it as making decisions with the person, not for the person, and notes it can be formal, through a written agreement, or informal. Under supported decision making the person keeps their legal authority. The definition does not, by itself, give a supporter power to sign for the person or to see records the person has not agreed to share.

Other alternatives do transfer some authority, within limits. Under section 145C.02, a person with the capacity to do so may make a health care directive containing health care instructions, a health care power of attorney naming an agent, or both. Unless the directive says otherwise, the agent decides only once the attending physician, advanced practice registered nurse or physician assistant determines the person lacks decision-making capacity. The statutory short form power of attorney in section 523.23 grants authority over financial and property matters, and its own notice states that it does not grant any power to make health care decisions. A representative payee is someone the Social Security Administration appoints to manage Social Security or SSI payments for a beneficiary who cannot manage them; that role reaches those benefits and nothing more. The court self-help sheet also names appropriate technological assistance and community or residential services as alternatives to weigh.

The trade-offs are real. Some alternatives, such as a directive or a power of attorney, must be made while the person has capacity to make them, so timing matters and earlier planning keeps more options open. Supported decision making depends on people the person trusts and chooses. DHS's December 2025 final report found that most people who put a less restrictive alternative in place during the grant period used tools such as health care directives, that few written supported decision-making agreements were completed partly because support networks take time to build, and that some people had no family, friends or professionals available to serve as supporters. A person who is isolated, new to Minnesota or estranged from family may have fewer paths away from guardianship. That is a system gap leaders can see and name.

For staff, the working rule is to read the arrangement, not the description of it. When someone says they are a person's power of attorney or health care agent, ask to see what the document covers and whether it is in effect, and follow the procedures your area uses for verifying authority. A financial power of attorney does not decide where someone lives or what health care they receive. A supporter under an informal arrangement speaks with the person, not instead of the person. If a document is unclear or the people involved disagree about what it allows, that is a legal question. Route it to the person, who may want their own attorney, and route agency questions to legal counsel or the person or area responsible, rather than interpreting the document yourself.
lessons.keyPoint: Each alternative covers specific decisions and has its own limits and starting point. Read the actual document or arrangement before treating anyone as a decision-maker, and send disputes about what it allows to people who can answer legal questions.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{CASE_MANAGER}} is coordinating with a provider about a person who wants to move closer to a sibling. The person's cousin calls and says, "I'm the power of attorney, and the move isn't happening." The person has told {{CASE_MANAGER}} they want to move and that the cousin helps with bills. No document is in the file.
lessons.question: What is the best next step for {{CASE_MANAGER}}?
choices: Pause the move planning, since a power of attorney has legal authority and the cousin may know about risks the person has not shared.
Proceed with the move as the person wants, since the cousin's phone call does not create authority and the person is clearly the decision-maker.
Ask to see the document and what it covers, keep planning with the person, and send any dispute to those who handle legal questions.
feedback: Pausing on a phone claim treats an unseen document as if it covered every decision. A statutory short form power of attorney covers financial and property matters, so the person's own wishes about where to live should not stop on that claim alone.
The person's wishes should guide the planning, but deciding on your own that no authority exists also skips a step. Seeing the document settles the question with evidence rather than assumption.
This keeps the person at the center, tests the claim against the document, and sends any real disagreement about authority to people equipped to answer it, without interpreting the law yourself.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a time you took someone's description of their role or authority at face value, at work or elsewhere. What would checking the actual document have changed, and how could you ask for it respectfully?
lessons.action: Make a one-page reference for your own use that lists supported decision making, a health care directive, a statutory short form power of attorney and a representative payee. For each, write which decisions it covers, when it takes effect and one question you would ask to confirm it. Check it against the sources in this course.

check.question: According to Minnesota Statutes section 523.23, what does the statutory short form power of attorney not cover?
check.correct: Health care decisions, which require a health care directive under chapter 145C.
wrong: Banking and real property transactions on the person's behalf.
Claims, litigation and records related to the person's property.
check.feedback: The form's own notice states that it does not grant power to make health care decisions. Banking, real property, claims and records are among the financial and property matters it can cover.

lessons.title: Rights a person keeps under guardianship
objectives: Identify the rights Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-120 guarantees to a person subject to guardianship.
Explain the conditions that apply before a guardian may restrict a person's communication or visitors.
Describe how a guardianship can be modified or ended under section 524.5-317.
Respond to a guardian's instruction that appears to limit a retained right without deciding the legal question yourself.
lessons.teaching:
A guardianship order limits some rights. It does not erase the person. Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-120 provides that a person subject to guardianship keeps all rights not restricted by court order, and it lists rights the court must enforce. They include treatment with dignity and respect, due weight to the person's past and current wishes, including medical, cultural and religious preferences, participation in health care decisions, and control of all aspects of life unless the court specifically delegates that power. The list also covers personal privacy, care and social and recreational activities, employment and education within available resources, consultation about personal property and about matters of image and name, the right to marry and have children unless court approval is required, and the right to vote unless the court restricts it.

Several rights speak directly to daily practice. The person may communicate with others, including through visitors, phone calls, mail and electronic messages. Under section 524.5-120, a guardian may restrict that contact only with good cause to believe it is necessary because the interaction poses a substantial risk of significant physical, psychological or financial harm and no other means can avoid or reduce that harm. Less restrictive options, such as supervised visits or limited calls, come first, and the guardian must give written notice, including to the court and the person, within 48 hours. The person may ask the court to remove or change the restriction. The person may ask the court to prevent or start a change in where they live, and section 524.5-313 lets the person or any interested person petition the court about a change in abode. The person may petition the court at any time to end or modify the guardianship or to challenge decisions made under it, and has the right to be represented by an attorney in those proceedings.

Guardianship is not meant to be permanent by design. Under section 524.5-317, any person interested in the person's welfare may petition to terminate or modify a guardianship. The court may terminate it when the person no longer needs a guardian's help or protection, or modify it when the powers granted are excessive or insufficient or the person's capacity has changed. Once a petitioner makes a prima facie case for termination, the court must end the guardianship unless continuing it is proven to be in the person's best interest. DHS's December 2025 final report described people whose rights were restored or whose guardianships ended through supported decision-making programs. It also noted that some guardians did not support petitions to remove guardianship.

The hard case for staff is an instruction from a guardian that seems to limit a retained right: a guardian says a person may not see a friend, attend a faith community or use a phone. You are not the court, and you cannot rule on whether the instruction is lawful. You can ask what the order says and whether a restriction was made with the required notice, record what the person wants in their own words, and raise the concern with your supervisor and the people responsible for the person's services. A person who disagrees with a guardian can be told, accurately, that they may petition the court and may have an attorney. If you suspect maltreatment of a vulnerable adult, section 626.557 requires mandated reporters to report immediately to the common entry point, whatever the guardianship status.
lessons.keyPoint: A person subject to guardianship keeps every right the court has not restricted, including communication, privacy, voting unless restricted, and the right to petition the court at any time. Staff record the person's wishes and raise concerns; the court decides disputes.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, who coordinates a peer support group, tells {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} that a group member subject to guardianship has stopped attending. The member later messaged that their guardian said the group was "a bad influence" and took the member's phone. The member wants to come back. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} does not know what the guardianship order says.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} respond?
choices: Tell {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} that a guardian controls the member's activities, so the group should respect the decision and wait for the guardian to call.
Explain the member's retained rights, suggest the member may petition the court, and route the concern to the people responsible for services.
Contact the guardian directly to explain that taking a phone violates the bill of rights and ask that it be returned to the member today.
feedback: This assumes the order covers everything. Communication and interaction with others are retained rights unless restricted under the statute's conditions, and the member's own wishes deserve a response.

This gives accurate public information, respects the limits of the role and moves the concern toward people who can look at the order and the member's services. Any suspicion of maltreatment would also be reported.
The concern is serious, but declaring a violation without seeing the order is a legal judgment. It can also escalate conflict in ways that leave the member with fewer options.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider which of the rights in section 524.5-120 you would find hardest to lose, and which you think are most often overlooked in services. What does that tell you about where to look in your own work?
lessons.action: Read the full list of rights in Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-120. Choose two that your team's work touches, such as communication or participation in health care decisions, and write down how your current forms or practices make room for the person's own voice on those matters. Share one improvement with your team.

check.question: Under section 524.5-120, when may a guardian restrict a person's communication with others?
check.correct: With good cause, a substantial risk of significant harm, less restrictive options tried first, and written notice within 48 hours.
wrong: Whenever the guardian believes a relationship is not in the person's best interest and records the reason.
Only after the court holds a hearing and issues a new order limiting all of the person's contacts.
check.feedback: The statute allows a restriction only under specific conditions: good cause, a substantial risk of significant harm that nothing else can avoid, less restrictive options first, and written notice within 48 hours. A guardian's general disapproval is not enough, and the statute does not require a new hearing for every restriction.

lessons.title: Supporting the person's own decisions in daily work
objectives: Use practices that keep the person as the first and primary voice in decisions about their life.
Distinguish sharing public information from giving legal advice, and route legal questions accordingly.
Record the person's preference and the source of any decision-maker's authority in the same place.
Review team forms, templates and habits that defer to a guardian or family member when the person keeps the right to decide.
lessons.teaching:
Most of the difference between support and substitution happens in ordinary moments. Who is addressed first in a meeting, whose signature a form asks for, which phone number goes into the file, whether information arrives in a format the person can use. These habits often defer to a guardian, a family member or a provider out of efficiency or caution, even when the person keeps the right to decide. The law sets the outer boundaries. Daily practice decides whether the person's authority within those boundaries is real.

Start with the person. Speak to them directly and first, even when another person has legal authority over some decisions. Ask who they want involved and in what role, and give information in their preferred language and format, with time to consider it. Supported decision making, as Minnesota law defines it, is help understanding the nature and consequences of a decision and, when the person wishes, help communicating it. Staff can offer the same kind of support: breaking a choice into parts, explaining consequences in plain language, checking understanding and asking what matters most. When a guardian does hold authority over a matter, the statute still requires due weight to the person's past and current wishes, so the person's preference belongs in the record next to the decision, along with the source of the decision-maker's authority.

Know the line between information and advice. Sharing public information is part of the job: the text of a statute, the court's self-help sheet on alternatives, the fact that a person may petition the court or have an attorney, or the name of a supported decision-making resource your area has approved for referral. Telling someone what they should file, how a court will rule, whether a document is valid, or which alternative is right for them is legal advice. Route those questions to the person, who may want their own attorney, or to court self-help services, and route questions about DHS's own obligations to legal counsel or the person or area responsible. If you are unsure which side of the line a question falls on, say so and route it.

Leaders own the system around these moments. Review forms and templates that ask only for a guardian's or family member's signature on matters the person may decide. Check whether case notes and data systems record the person's preference separately from the decision. Look at where guardianship shows up as a default in your materials and referrals, and at who has the fewest alternatives available, such as people without a network of supporters. DHS's December 2025 final report recommended sharing supported decision-making tools across Minnesota and improving guardianship data, which signals that the evidence base is still developing. Be modest about what any single change will achieve, measure what you can, and keep asking the people affected whether the process left the decision with them.
lessons.keyPoint: Support keeps the person as the decision-maker; substitution quietly takes the decision away. Address the person first, record their preference alongside any decision, share public information freely, and route legal advice to people who can give it.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} reviews a team template for service planning meetings. It lists the guardian, if any, as the first attendee and the only required signature. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} points out that several people the team works with have limited guardianships that leave decisions about daily activities and work with the person, and that the template gives them no place to record their own choices.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} do?
choices: Revise the template to list the person first, record their choices and note what any order covers, then check it with the owner.
Leave the template as it is but remind staff in a team meeting to ask people about their preferences before the guardian signs the plan.
Remove the guardian signature line entirely, since many guardianships are limited and the person should be the only one who signs the plan.
feedback: This builds the person's authority into the tool rather than relying on memory, and it reflects that an order defines what a guardian decides. Checking with the template's owner keeps the change within the right process.
A reminder helps for a while, but the template still signals that the guardian's view comes first and gives the person's choices nowhere to live. Tools tend to outlast reminders.

This corrects for limited orders but ignores guardianships that do cover planning decisions. Some signatures may be required, and that is a question for the template's owner and counsel, not a blanket removal.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about a recent meeting or conversation where someone's decision was discussed. Who was addressed first, whose words were written down, and what would the person themselves say about how it went?
lessons.action: Choose one routine moment in your work, such as a meeting agenda, a form or a phone script. Rewrite it so the person is addressed first, their preference has a place to be recorded, and any other decision-maker's authority is noted with its source. Test it with a colleague and, where your role allows, with someone who uses it.

check.question: Which of these is sharing public information rather than giving legal advice?
check.correct: Telling a person that Minnesota law lets them petition the court at any time to modify or end a guardianship.
wrong: Telling a family that a supported decision-making agreement will be enough to avoid guardianship in their situation.
Telling a person that their cousin's power of attorney is not valid and can be ignored.
check.feedback: Stating what the statute provides is public information. Predicting the outcome of someone's situation or judging whether a document is valid is legal advice, which belongs with the person's attorney, court resources or legal counsel.

cards.back: Under Minnesota Statutes 524.5-310, clear and convincing evidence of incapacity and specific findings that less restrictive means, including supported decision making and technology, will not meet the person's needs.
Any power a guardianship order does not specifically grant remains with the person. The order, not the fact of guardianship, says who decides a given matter.
Help from people the person chooses to understand the nature and consequences of decisions and, when the person wishes, to communicate them. The person keeps legal authority.
Under chapter 145C, instructions, a named health care agent or both. Unless it says otherwise, the agent decides only after a qualified clinician finds the person lacks decision-making capacity.

cards.front: Statutory short form power of attorney
cards.back: Authority over financial and property matters under section 523.23. Its notice states that it grants no power to make health care decisions.
Under section 524.5-120, every right not restricted by court order, including dignity, privacy, communication, voting unless restricted, and petitioning the court at any time.

Under section 524.5-317, an interested person may petition. After a prima facie case for termination, the court ends the guardianship unless continuing it is proven to be in the person's best interest.
Sharing what the law and court resources say is information. Predicting an outcome, judging a document's validity or recommending what to file is legal advice to route elsewhere.

aid.heading: Before guardianship comes up
items: Check your materials for wording that presents guardianship as expected or required.
Share neutral public information that alternatives exist and must be considered first.
Point legal questions to the person's own attorney or court self-help resources.

aid.heading: When someone claims authority
items: Ask to see the order or document and what it covers, and follow your area's procedures for verifying it.
Remember that powers not granted by the order stay with the person.
Keep planning with the person while authority is confirmed.
Send disputes about what a document allows to legal counsel or the person or area responsible.

aid.heading: Protect retained rights
items: Record the person's wishes in their own words alongside any decision someone else makes.
Tell a person who disagrees with a guardian that they may petition the court and may have an attorney.
Raise concerns about a restriction with your supervisor and the people responsible for services.
Report suspected maltreatment immediately to the common entry point, whatever the guardianship status.

aid.heading: Build support into the system
items: Address the person first in meetings, forms and phone scripts.
Give information in the person's language and format, with time to decide.
Review templates that ask only for a guardian's or family member's signature.
Notice who has the fewest alternatives, such as people without supporters, and raise that gap.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310, Findings; order of appointment
sources.note: Supports the clear and convincing evidence standard, the less restrictive means requirement including supported decision making, the specific findings, the limits on powers and the rule that powers not granted stay with the person. Courts apply it; staff do not.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-102, Definitions
sources.note: Supports the definitions of incapacitated person (subdivision 6) and supported decision making (subdivision 16a). It does not set out how supported decision-making agreements are made or recognized by third parties.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-120, Bill of rights for persons subject to guardianship or conservatorship
sources.note: Supports the list of retained rights, the conditions for restricting communication and the rights to petition the court and be represented by an attorney. Sections 524.5-303, 524.5-313 and 524.5-317, cited in the lessons, are linked from the same chapter.

sources.title: Minnesota Judicial Branch, State Court Administrator's Office: Less Restrictive Alternatives Available Prior to Guardianship (revised August 27, 2024)
sources.note: Supports the expectation that alternatives be seriously considered and meaningfully tried and describes health care directives, technology, supported decision making and community services. It is public self-help information, not legal advice; check for a newer version.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Supported Decision Making in Minnesota: Final Report to the Minnesota State Legislature (December 2025)
sources.note: Supports the findings on guardianship as a default, limited awareness of alternatives, grant outcomes, barriers such as a lack of supporters, and recommendations on tools and data. It evaluates five grantees and does not establish statewide outcomes.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 145C.02, Health care directive
sources.note: Supports what a health care directive may contain and when a health care agent's authority begins unless the directive says otherwise. Execution requirements are in other sections of chapter 145C.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 523.23, Statutory short form power of attorney
sources.note: Supports the financial and property matters the form covers and its notice that it grants no health care decision-making power. The representative payee description is from the Social Security Administration's representative payee page (ssa.gov/payee).
